sources.title: CLAM: Continuous Latent Action Models for Robot Learning from Unlabeled Demonstrations

sectionsRead: IV. Continuous Latent Action Models; A. Latent Action Model Training; B. Latent Action Policy Training; Algorithms 1–2 (pp. 3–4)
VII. Conclusion, including video and embodiment limitations (p. 7)

synopsis: CLAM learns continuous action codes from robot observation transitions, grounds them with limited action-labeled data, then imitates expert videos in that latent space. Deployment uses a policy and action decoder; future-observation prediction serves training. Its strongest evidence concerns action-label scarcity within one robot embodiment, with several unresolved protocol details.

problem.text: How can a robot imitate task-specific demonstrations whose actions are withheld? CLAM separates a large observation corpus, a small action-labeled grounding set, and observation-only expert demonstrations. Experiments isolate action inference using robot data in a single-task, single-embodiment setting. Section III allows some task-specific demonstrations within the labeled mixture; the strongest “no expert labels” wording must therefore be read alongside the purely suboptimal-data ablation.

contributions.text: Combines continuous latent inverse dynamics with a jointly trained action decoder that remains in the execution pipeline.
The authors argue that this combination makes latent-action relabeling practical for continuous control; the factorial MetaWorld ablation directly tests these two choices.

outputs: Executable continuous actions from the deployed policy and decoder

steps.name: Infer and reconstruct transitions
steps.detail: The latent IDM f_phi observes consecutive observations plus history and produces z_t. The FDM g_psi predicts the next observation from history and z_t. Reconstruction trains a compact, continuous transition code; the source describes this as a low-level, potentially state-dependent action representation, not a skill label.

steps.name: Ground the latent space
steps.detail: The decoder p_omega maps z_t to the environment action without observing the scene. Reconstruction updates the IDM/FDM; action regression updates both the decoder and IDM on labeled batches. Thus labeled supervision shapes the representation itself.

steps.name: Relabel and imitate
steps.detail: The pretrained IDM annotates expert observation pairs. A separate policy pi_theta learns their latent targets by mean-squared error. The FDM is discarded; Figure 1 marks the pretrained IDM as locked during policy training.

training.text: Image CLAM patchifies 64×64 RGB frames into sixteen 16×16 patches, applies spatial then temporal attention, and predicts latent actions from per-frame CLS tokens. The decoder also cross-attends to latent actions. The policy description separately specifies ResNet18 image features and an ACT-like transformer decoder.

Appendix defaults: 500,000 CLAM updates, decoder training every two updates, decoder batch size 128, both loss weights 1, latent dimension 16 and context length 2. Transformer defaults include three encoder/decoder layers, model dimension 256, four heads and dropout 0.1.

inference.text: Algorithm 2 repeatedly observes, predicts a latent action, decodes it, and steps the environment. It performs no predicted-video search or FDM rollout. The implementation predicts five-action chunks spanning one second; how overlapping chunks are executed or refreshed is not specified.

equations.explanation: The source’s unnumbered objective combines next-observation reconstruction with action regression. Hats denote predictions; o is an observation, a an environment action, t the timestep, and beta the loss-balancing hyperparameter. The two terms use unlabeled and labeled batches respectively.
The policy predicts the continuous latent action z_t supplied by the pretrained IDM; the hat denotes its prediction. Expert environment actions are not policy targets.

reasoning.text: The recorded categories are all unassigned, so no existing quadrant claim can be confirmed. Architecturally, CLAM is a multicomponent latent inverse-dynamics pipeline with a training-time forward model and separate deployed policy/decoder. Joint training does not establish a One Model architecture or joint future/action generation at inference. This is an assessment for later classification, not a catalog change.

discussionQuestions: Would continuous codes still help when all baselines receive identical representation pretraining?
How much task-relevant transition coverage must random play provide for reliable grounding?

results.setting: HalfCheetah and Hopper; medium-expert pretraining data and suboptimal labeled trajectories.
results.interpretation: These are returns, not success rates. The supplied source does not define the ± statistic or a separate state-evaluation rollout count.

results.setting: Assembly, Bin Picking, Peg Insert and Shelf Place; replay-buffer pretraining and held-out random-medium labeled data.
results.interpretation: CLAM exceeds VPT across these tasks but does not exceed the privileged reference. Table I’s overall average mixes returns and success rates.

results.setting: Four manipulation tasks; Figure 2 specifies 50 evaluation rollouts across three seeds and 100 labeled trajectories.
results.value: ST-ViViT-CLAM: 76%, reported in the results text.
results.comparison: LAPO: 9%; LAPA: 20%, under the paper’s limited, non-fully-expert labeled-data regime.
results.interpretation: This is executed simulated control. The caption and appendix disagree on labeled-data count; the caption also names variants absent from the plotted legend.

results.setting: Table II, Assembly column; discrete/continuous codes crossed with joint decoder training (JT).
results.comparison: Continuous without JT: 0.28 ± 0.04; discrete without JT: 0.15 ± 0.03; discrete + JT: 0.14 ± 0.04.
results.interpretation: Joint grounding helps strongly with continuous codes here. Table II’s caption compares rows 2→3 while changing both factors; rows 1→3 and 3→4 are cleaner contrasts.

results.setting: Block, Button, Microwave and Slide Pot; ten trials per task with partial/full credit of 0.5/1.
results.interpretation: These totals are not counts of fully successful trials. No per-trial outcomes, uncertainty interval or significance test is supplied.

results.setting: Figure 4 left: latent dimensions 2, 4, 8 and 16; MetaWorld’s physical action dimension is four.
results.comparison: Dimension eight exceeds dimension four despite both representing the same control task.
results.interpretation: Matching the motor-action dimension is insufficient in this experiment; larger is not monotonically better.

limitations.text: Internet-video robustness and human-to-robot transfer remain future work. Expert robot demonstrations are still needed, with labels withheld. The conclusion’s broad “without expert teleoperation” wording exceeds this experimental scope.

The appendix lists 50 labeled MetaWorld trajectories versus Figure 2’s 100, and real expert trajectories as “30/50” without task assignment versus approximately 30 per task in Section V. Figure 4’s scaling axis says D_unlabeled, while its caption describes relabeling with a pretrained CLAM and Section VI’s heading says D_unlabeled-expert. These inconsistencies remain unresolved.

BC-Expert has privileged action labels but lacks CLAM’s larger-corpus pretraining. Near-parity therefore does not isolate the causal value of latent actions or establish that expert labels are unnecessary under matched pretraining. The authors explicitly leave causal attribution open.

reproduction.text: Preserve separate corpus, grounding and expert datasets. Table VI lists 1,000 unlabeled and 20 expert trajectories for each simulated domain; the real setup uses approximately 50,000 unlabeled and 5,000 labeled transitions. The WidowX setup uses external D435 and over-the-shoulder C920 cameras; native action dimensions are 3/6/4/7 for Hopper/HalfCheetah/MetaWorld/WidowX.

The supplied recipe omits optimizer, learning rate, policy-update count, training compute/hardware and software versions. The return cutoff used to select random trajectories is unnamed. Resolve dataset counts, return normalization and encoder initialization before treating a run as an exact reproduction; Section II’s no-off-the-shelf-model wording coexists with Section V’s pretrained ResNet.
